overview: Fortescue is the world's fourth-largest iron ore producer, operating an integrated mine-rail-port system in Western Australia's Pilbara region that shipped a record 201.3 million tonnes in FY2026 (June year-end). Founded in 2003 by Executive Chairman Dr Andrew Forrest, the group reports two segments: Metals (iron ore mining, processing and export, ~99% of group revenue) and Energy (Fortescue Zero decarbonisation technology, green hydrogen R&D and, increasingly, Pilbara renewable-energy infrastructure intended to lower the miner's own operating costs). Fortescue is almost entirely a single-commodity, single-region business selling into a China-dominated seaborne iron ore market, funded by one of the lowest hematite cost positions in the industry.

business_model.summary: Fortescue makes money overwhelmingly from mining, processing, railing, shipping and selling iron ore (Hematite and, since 2022-23, Iron Bridge Magnetite concentrate) to steel mills, predominantly in China. Revenue is a function of shipped volumes, the achieved discount/premium to the Platts 61-62% Fe CFR index, and freight recovered through shipping revenue. The separately reported Energy segment is a small, currently loss-making technology and green-infrastructure business (motorsport/cleantech via Fortescue Zero and wind-turbine components via newly acquired Nabrawind) that in FY2026 generated only US$136 million of revenue (0.8% of group revenue) against a US$422 million Underlying EBITDA loss, while absorbing meaningful capital (US$88 million of capex in FY2026, down sharply from US$312 million in FY2025 after the pipeline was cut back) — a capital allocation choice framed by management as building the Green Grid that will lower Metals' own C1 costs (targeted ~20% reduction; ~US$100 million/year of fossil-fuel savings expected from FY27) rather than as a standalone profit centre.

revenue_streams.name: Hematite iron ore sales
revenue_streams.description: 192.3Mt shipped in FY2026 at a realised price of US$91/dmt (FY25: US$85/dmt), generating US$14,966 million of iron ore revenue (Metals segment). Sold via long-term contracts, portside sales in China (via Fortescue Trading Shanghai) and seaborne spot in both USD and RMB.

revenue_streams.name: Shipping revenue (freight)
revenue_streams.description: US$1,733 million in FY2026 (FY25: US$1,415 million), reflecting Fortescue's owned VLOC fleet (8 vessels, ~10% of shipping needs) plus chartered and FOB shipments; grows with elevated global shipping rates.

revenue_streams.name: Iron Bridge Magnetite concentrate
revenue_streams.trend: growing off a low base, capped by ramp-up
revenue_streams.description: 9.0Mt shipped in FY2026 (100% basis, +27% YoY) at a realised price of US$120/dmt (65% Fe), still well short of the 22Mtpa nameplate; FY2027 guidance of only 11-14Mt confirms a multi-year ramp-up (full capacity not expected before ~2028) and a US$750m pre-tax impairment was booked in FY2026 against the CGU.

revenue_streams.name: Energy segment revenue
revenue_streams.description: US$136 million in FY2026 (+68% YoY off a low base), from Fortescue Zero's motorsport/cleantech products and Nabrawind's wind-turbine component sales; segment Underlying EBITDA was a US$422 million loss (FY25: US$741 million loss) — narrowing but still deeply negative, funded by Metals cash flow, not customer revenue.

business_model.customer_type: B2B — global steel mills, overwhelmingly Chinese, purchasing under long-term contracts, portside China sales and seaborne spot
business_model.geographic_mix: Mining and export 100% Western Australia (Pilbara); revenue destination overwhelmingly China (historically ~85-90% of shipments), with growth exploration/development interests in Gabon (Belinga hematite), Peru (Cañariaco copper, acquired via Alta Copper in Jan-2026), Kazakhstan, Canada and Argentina still in pre-development/exploration stage and immaterial to current revenue
business_model.margin_profile: FY2026 Underlying EBITDA margin 51% at the group level (54% for Metals alone, down from 56% in FY2025), among the highest in global mining; Hematite C1 unit cost of US$18.74/wmt (FY25: US$17.99/wmt) remains toward the bottom of the global cost curve, though FY2027 guidance of US$20.50-21.75/wmt signals continued cost inflation from diesel, FX and lower ore grades/strip ratio.

main_competitors: Simandou consortia (Guinea — Rio Tinto/Chinalco SimFer and WCS/Baowu-backed projects, first major new low-cost supply source in decades)
Roy Hill, Mineral Resources (MinRes), Hancock/Atlas Iron and other smaller Pilbara producers
competitive_position.market_position: Fourth-largest iron ore producer globally by volume (~201Mt shipped in FY2026), the largest of the 'second tier' behind BHP, Rio Tinto and Vale; roughly 18-20% of the seaborne Pilbara export market and a mid-single-digit percentage of total global seaborne iron ore supply. Product mix is skewed to lower/mid-grade Hematite (56-58% Fe), which trades at a structural discount to benchmark (61-62% Fe) and to Vale/Iron Bridge higher-grade product, a discount that management is actively managing via product mix changes (phasing out West Pilbara Fines for a new 55% Fe 'Fortune Fines' product).
competitive_position.market_share: Approximately 18-20% of Pilbara/Australian iron ore exports; global seaborne iron ore market share in the mid-single digits behind Vale, Rio Tinto and BHP

moat_factors.description: Wholly owned, purpose-built 760km rail network, Herb Elliott Port (>200Mtpa capacity, 5 berths, 3 shiploaders), and 3 mining hubs (Chichester, Western, Solomon) integrated end-to-end and centrally managed from the 'Hive' remote-operations centre in Perth. This vertical integration is the primary driver of Fortescue's C1 cost position (US$18.74/wmt in FY2026) near the bottom of the global cost curve, a durable structural advantage replicated only by BHP and Rio Tinto within the Pilbara.

Net gearing of only 4% and net debt of US$857 million against US$5.1 billion cash on hand at 30 June 2026 gives Fortescue capacity to sustain capex and dividends through a down-cycle better than most single-commodity peers of similar size.

moat_factors.factor: Established customer relationships and marketing network
moat_factors.description: Two decades of long-term contracts with Chinese steel mills, plus a wholly owned trading entity (Fortescue Trading Shanghai) enabling direct RMB-denominated portside sales — a flexible go-to-market advantage relative to smaller Pilbara juniors.

The Pilbara 'Green Grid' (1.1GW solar under construction, wind at Nullagine, 4-5GWh of planned battery storage) is targeted to cut C1 costs by up to 20%/wmt and remove ~1 billion litres of diesel annually, with ~US$100 million/year of fossil-fuel savings expected once online — a genuine potential moat extension if delivered on budget and schedule, but currently a promise rather than a realised advantage.

moat_factors.factor: Brand / reputation with a single dominant founder-owner
moat_factors.description: Dr Andrew Forrest's ~36% shareholding and high public profile drive strategic conviction (Real Zero commitment, rapid capital deployment) but also concentrate key-person and governance risk; strategy pivots (e.g., the FY2025 hydrogen retrenchment) have at times been abrupt.

weaknesses: Single commodity (iron ore, ~99% of revenue) and single region (Pilbara, Western Australia) concentration — no geographic or commodity diversification in current production, unlike BHP and Rio Tinto's multi-commodity portfolios

Lower average ore grade (56-58% Fe Hematite) than benchmark and than Vale/Iron Bridge product, meaning Fortescue structurally realises a discount to the Platts index (FY2026 Hematite realised price US$91/dmt vs 61% Fe CFR Platts index of US$103/dmt) that widens when low-grade discounts blow out in soft markets

Iron Bridge Magnetite project has materially underperformed design intent — 9Mt shipped in FY2026 versus 22Mtpa nameplate, a US$750 million pre-tax impairment booked, and full ramp-up not expected until ~2028 — undermining the higher-grade diversification thesis

Energy segment has consumed billions of dollars in cumulative capex and opex for minimal revenue and continues to run large EBITDA losses (US$422 million in FY2026), a capital-allocation debate investors continue to have with management
Heavy reliance on China as the demand market exposes Fortescue disproportionately to Chinese property/steel-sector weakness and trade-policy shifts
Unresolved, potentially precedent-setting native title legal exposure (Yindjibarndi) with an unclear final compensation quantum

growth_drivers: Iron Bridge Magnetite ramp-up: even at a reduced pace (FY2027 guidance 11-14Mt against 22Mtpa nameplate), continued ramp-up of a higher-grade (65% Fe) product commanding a premium (US$120/dmt realised in FY2026) diversifies Fortescue's product mix over time, though the FY2026 impairment reset expectations materially lower
Life-of-mine extension via Blacksmith deposit inclusion in the Western Hub, adding 249Mt to reserves and improving mine sequencing/strip ratios, extending the low-cost Pilbara production base
Product mix optimisation — phasing out lower-value West Pilbara Fines for the new 55% Fe 'Fortune Fines' product, targeted to lower C1 unit costs and improve capital efficiency

Green Grid decarbonisation program (1.5GW solar, 900MW wind, 4-5GWh battery storage) — a genuine potential structural cost advantage (up to 20% C1 cost reduction targeted) if delivered, insulating Fortescue from diesel price volatility (~1 billion litres/year to be displaced)

Green Metal Project at Christmas Creek achieved first hot metal in August 2026, an early-stage but symbolically important proof point for Fortescue's ambition to produce lower-emissions metal from Pilbara ore, potentially opening a large new addressable market (management cites a hypothetical >A$170 billion Australian green-metals opportunity, though this is aspirational and pre-commercial)

Critical minerals/copper optionality via the Cañariaco project in Peru (acquired through Alta Copper, completed January 2026) and continued exploration in Gabon (Belinga hematite), Kazakhstan, Canada and Argentina — long-dated, high-optionality, low near-term earnings contribution

Disciplined capital allocation framework prioritising sustaining capex, then growth/decarbonisation, then shareholder returns via a 50-80% payout ratio dividend policy, supporting continued cash return to shareholders even through a softer pricing environment

business.risk: China steel demand and iron ore price cyclicality
business.description: Fortescue's earnings are almost entirely a function of Chinese steel production and the Platts 61-62% Fe CFR index. Consensus forecasts point to softer prices into 2026-2027 (median estimates in the US$85-100/t range, down from FY2026's realised US$91/dmt) as Chinese property-driven steel demand stays weak and Simandou (Guinea) supply ramps from ~15-20Mt in 2026 toward 120Mt by 2030, structurally pressuring the seaborne market Fortescue depends on.

Essentially 100% of current production and ~99% of revenue is Pilbara hematite/magnetite iron ore. Any Pilbara-specific operational disruption (weather, labour, infrastructure failure) or a structural de-rating of iron ore as a commodity has no offsetting diversification within the current production base.

Hematite's 56-58% Fe grade realises below the Platts benchmark; low-grade discounts have historically widened sharply in weak markets (as steel mills favour higher-grade ore to maximise blast-furnace productivity when margins are thin), which would disproportionately hurt Fortescue's realised price relative to BHP/Rio Tinto/Vale's higher-grade portfolios.

business.risk: Iron Bridge execution and asset-value risk
business.description: A US$750 million pre-tax (US$525 million post-tax) impairment was booked in FY2026 reflecting a revised ramp-up schedule; shipments of 9Mt in FY2026 remain well short of 22Mtpa nameplate, full capacity is not expected before ~2028, and technical issues including a leaking water-supply pipeline have added hundreds of millions in cost. Further downside revisions to the ramp-up schedule cannot be ruled out.

business.risk: Fortescue Energy capital allocation and returns
business.description: The Energy segment generated only US$136 million of revenue in FY2026 against a US$422 million EBITDA loss, following billions of dollars of cumulative investment and multiple write-downs in FY2025-26 (Gladstone Electrolyser Manufacturing Centre, Arizona Hydrogen Project, Fortescue Zero UK manufacturing assets). While the pivot toward Pilbara-focused Green Grid infrastructure (which reduces Metals' own costs rather than seeking third-party energy revenue) is more capital-disciplined than the earlier global hydrogen ambitions, the segment's ultimate return on invested capital remains unproven and management retains wide discretion over how much further capital to commit.

financial.description: Management discloses that a 1-cent move in AUD:USD shifts Hematite C1 cost by ~US$0.16/wmt, and a US$10/barrel diesel move shifts it by ~US$0.20/wmt; FY2027 guidance assumes AUD:USD of 0.70. A stronger AUD or renewed oil-price spikes (the Middle East conflict already elevated diesel costs in FY2026) would directly compress margins.

FY2027 Hematite C1 cost guidance of US$20.50-21.75/wmt represents a 9-16% increase over FY2026's US$18.74/wmt, reflecting higher strip ratios, lower ore grades at some pits, and inflation — an erosion of Fortescue's cost-curve advantage if it continues.

Metals capex guidance of US$3.7-4.7 billion plus Energy capex of ~US$150 million and net opex of ~US$300 million for FY2027 is a substantial call on FY2026's US$3.2 billion of free cash flow; sustained high growth/decarbonisation capex alongside a 50-80% dividend payout could pressure the balance sheet if iron ore prices fall meaningfully.

Debt is spread across USD senior notes/green bonds, an RMB-denominated syndicated term loan (RMB14.2bn, drawn September 2025) and a secured VLOC term loan; net gearing is low (4%) but the multi-currency structure adds refinancing and FX-translation complexity.

regulatory.description: In May 2026 the Federal Court ordered compensation of approximately A$150.3 million for cultural loss plus economic loss to the Yindjibarndi Traditional Owners over Fortescue's Solomon mining hub, finding 124 culturally significant sites were destroyed. Fortescue has fully provided A$150.4 million (US$103.6 million) as a legal compensation expense in FY2026 (the US$104m pre-tax / US$73m post-tax 'significant item'). However, all three parties — Fortescue, the WA Government and the Yindjibarndi Aboriginal Corporation (which sought closer to A$1.8 billion) — filed separate appeals, leaving Australia's largest-ever native title compensation award legally unsettled as of September 2026. The ultimate quantum, and precedent for other native title claims across Fortescue's and the industry's tenements, remains a material open risk.

regulatory.risk: Mining royalties and Australian resources policy
regulatory.description: Fortescue pays a 7.5% government royalty on Hematite (5% concession for beneficiated fines) and 5% on Magnetite concentrate; royalty and resources-tax settings in Western Australia are periodically revisited politically.

regulatory.risk: Climate/decarbonisation policy and diesel fuel tax credit settings
regulatory.description: Executive Chairman Andrew Forrest has publicly criticised Australia's uncapped diesel fuel tax credit as favouring imported fossil fuels over Fortescue's renewable investment; any change (or lack of change) to these settings affects the relative economics of the Green Grid investment case.

Ongoing mine development (e.g., Blacksmith, hub expansions) requires environmental and heritage approvals; heritage-site exclusions have already reduced reserve estimates at some deposits, and further approval delays or heritage disputes (compounded by the Yindjibarndi precedent) could affect mine plans and timing.

macro.description: China's weak property sector continues to erode a key pillar of steel demand; Chinese port iron ore inventories are near record levels (~160Mt), a bearish demand-side indicator for price.

Simandou is expected to add 15-20Mt of new high-grade seaborne supply in 2026, scaling toward 40-50Mt in 2027 and up to 120Mt by 2030 — a structural supply-side headwind that could pressure prices and further disadvantage Fortescue's lower-grade product versus premium high-grade alternatives.

Shipping costs rose from US$1,432 million to US$1,701 million in FY2026 on elevated freight rates and geopolitical disruption; continued volatility in global shipping (e.g., Middle East conflict effects) directly affects delivered costs and thus margins on a large share of tonnes.

As a high-beta, cyclical commodity equity with a large dividend yield, Fortescue's valuation is sensitive to risk-free rate moves and broader risk appetite for cyclicals, though the low net gearing (4%) limits direct balance-sheet interest rate exposure.

execution.risk: Delivering the Green Grid and Iron Bridge on time and on budget
execution.description: Both the decarbonisation infrastructure buildout and the Iron Bridge ramp-up have already experienced delays, cost overruns and impairments; continued execution slippage would undermine both the promised C1 cost-reduction thesis and the magnetite diversification thesis simultaneously.

Fortescue significantly scaled back its global green hydrogen ambitions in 2024-2025 (cancelling the Arizona Hydrogen Project and PEM50 Queensland project, cutting ~90 Perth/Gladstone jobs, moving Fortescue Zero away from in-house manufacturing to R&D-only), booking further write-downs in FY2026. Repeated strategy reversals raise questions about the durability of whatever Energy strategy management settles on next and the capital already sunk into abandoned initiatives.

Elizabeth Gaines (Executive Director) resigned effective 30 June 2026, with Sigrid Kaag to join the Board subject to regulatory approval; the CEO structure is split between Dino Otranto (Metals and Operations) and Gus Pichot (Growth and Energy), a dual-CEO model that requires clear alignment given the material capital-allocation trade-offs between the two segments.

Dr Andrew Forrest's dominant strategic influence and shareholding is a source of both conviction and key-person risk; major strategic pivots (Real Zero commitment, hydrogen retrenchment, Green Grid acceleration) have originated substantially from his personal advocacy.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global seaborne iron ore faces a softening multi-year outlook: consensus 2026 price forecasts cluster around US$85-100/t (down from FY2026's realised US$91/dmt for Fortescue's product), driven by stagnant Chinese steel/property demand and a wave of new supply from Guinea's Simandou project (15-20Mt in 2026, scaling to ~120Mt by 2030). Chinese port inventories near record levels (~160Mt) reinforce the bearish near-term demand/supply balance, even as China's renewed focus on infrastructure and advanced manufacturing provides a partial offset.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High. Iron ore is a classic cyclical commodity tied closely to Chinese steel production, itself tied to Chinese property and infrastructure investment; Fortescue's earnings, cash flow and dividends swing materially with the Platts CFR index and low-grade discount dynamics.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low direct balance-sheet sensitivity given net gearing of only 4%, but moderate indirect sensitivity via commodity-cyclical equity valuation multiples and via Chinese monetary/fiscal stimulus settings that drive steel demand.
key_input_costs: Diesel and fuel (US$10/barrel move impacts Hematite C1 cost by ~US$0.20/wmt; Middle East conflict already elevated FY2026 costs)
AUD:USD exchange rate (1-cent move impacts Hematite C1 cost by ~US$0.16/wmt)
Labour costs and inflation across the Pilbara workforce
Global shipping/freight rates (Very Large Ore Carrier charter and Free-on-Board rates)
Capital equipment (haul trucks, excavators, rail and port infrastructure) subject to global mining-equipment supply and cost cycles
macro_factors.currency_exposure: Reports in US dollars (iron ore is a USD-denominated global commodity) while incurring a large share of operating costs in Australian dollars, creating a natural cost-side AUD exposure that management explicitly guides on (AUD:USD assumed at 0.70 for FY2027); debt is a multi-currency mix of USD notes/bonds and an RMB-denominated syndicated term loan.

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results: record shipments of 201.3Mt, revenue up 9% to US$16,966 million, Underlying EBITDA up 9% to US$8,635 million (51% margin), but statutory NPAT down 15% to US$2,870 million due to a US$750 million pre-tax Iron Bridge impairment and a US$104 million Yindjibarndi legal compensation provision; Underlying NPAT rose 3% to US$3,468 million. Final dividend of 46 Australian cents declared (total FY2026 dividends of 108 cents, a 65% payout ratio).

FY2027 guidance issued: iron ore shipments of 197-207Mt (including 11-14Mt Iron Bridge on a 100% basis), Hematite C1 cost of US$20.50-21.75/wmt (up from US$18.74/wmt in FY2026), Metals capex of US$3.7-4.7 billion, and Energy capex of ~US$150 million with net opex of ~US$300 million, based on an assumed AUD:USD of 0.70.

Federal Court ordered Fortescue to pay approximately A$150.3 million in cultural loss compensation (plus economic loss) to the Yindjibarndi Traditional Owners over destruction of 124 culturally significant sites at the Solomon mining hub — described as Australia's largest-ever native title compensation award. Fortescue fully provided for the amount in FY2026 accounts.

Fortescue, the Western Australian Government and the Yindjibarndi Aboriginal Corporation all filed separate appeals against the Federal Court decision (YNAC had sought ~A$1.8 billion), leaving the ultimate compensation amount unresolved as of mid-September 2026.

Iron Bridge impairment flagged in the June quarterly report ahead of full-year results: US$750 million pre-tax (US$525 million post-tax) write-down against the Iron Bridge magnetite Cash Generating Unit reflecting a revised ramp-up schedule and reduced production scenarios (22Mtpa nameplate not expected to be reached until around 2028); technical issues including a leaking water-supply pipeline contributed to cost overruns.
Completed acquisition of Alta Copper Corp, securing 100% ownership of the Cañariaco copper project in Peru, expanding Fortescue's critical minerals/copper diversification ambitions.
First hot metal achieved at the Green Metal Project, Christmas Creek — an early proof-of-concept step in Fortescue's green iron/green metal ambitions.

Continued scale-back of the global green hydrogen strategy: cancellation of the Arizona Hydrogen Project and Queensland PEM50 project (with further FY2026 write-downs of the Gladstone Electrolyser Manufacturing Centre and remaining Arizona plant components), ~90 job cuts in Perth/Gladstone in May 2025, and a shift of Fortescue Zero away from in-house manufacturing toward R&D-only, alongside a pivot of Energy capital toward Pilbara-focused Green Grid renewable infrastructure that directly reduces Metals segment costs.
recent_developments.impact: mixed (capital discipline improving, but reflects a costly earlier strategic miscalculation)

recent_developments.event: Shares traded near a 52-week low (~A$16.14-16.73) against a 52-week high of ~A$23.38, down roughly 27-30% from the high, amid soft iron ore prices and the stock trading ex-dividend; analyst sentiment mixed-to-cautious, with several sell-side price targets clustering around A$16-24 and at least one prominent 'Sell' rating (RaaS Group, mid-September 2026) arguing shares remain overpriced even after the pullback.
Elizabeth Gaines resigned from the Board effective 30 June 2026; Sigrid Kaag to be appointed as a Non-Executive Director subject to regulatory clearance.

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Full Year Results / Annual Report (20 August 2026)

items.target: 197-207 million tonnes, including 11-14Mt for Iron Bridge (100% basis)
items.notes: Range midpoint (~202Mt) is roughly flat with FY2026's record; Iron Bridge guidance of 11-14Mt is up from 9Mt shipped in FY2026 but still far below the 22Mtpa nameplate, confirming a multi-year ramp-up.

items.vs_prior: raised (cost guidance higher than FY2026 actual of US$18.74/wmt)
items.notes: Represents a 9-16% cost increase, attributed to diesel costs, FX, strip ratio and grade; guidance is based on an assumed AUD:USD of 0.70. Sensitivities disclosed: 1-cent AUD:USD move = ~US$0.16/wmt; US$10/barrel diesel move = ~US$0.20/wmt.

items.target: US$3.7-4.7 billion (Sustaining/hub development US$2.3-2.7bn; Decarbonisation US$0.9-1.3bn; Exploration/studies US$300-500m; Other projects US$150m)
items.vs_prior: broadly similar to FY2026 actual (US$3,552 million Metals capex)
items.notes: Decarbonisation capex range (US$0.9-1.3bn) is up materially from FY2026 actual (US$848m), reflecting acceleration of Green Grid solar/wind/battery/transmission build.

items.target: ~US$150 million capex; ~US$300 million net operating expenditure
items.vs_prior: capex roughly flat to slightly higher than FY2026 actual (US$88m); opex guidance implies continued but moderating Energy segment cash burn
items.notes: Materially smaller than the FY2025 Energy capex of US$312 million, reflecting the strategic scale-back of the hydrogen pipeline.

FY2026 total dividends of 108 Australian cents represented a 65% payout ratio, within the policy band; final FY2026 dividend of 46 Australian cents (fully franked) was lower than the FY2025 final of 60 cents, reflecting the FY2026 statutory NPAT decline from the Iron Bridge impairment and Yindjibarndi provision.

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEOs Dino Otranto for Metals/Operations and Gus Pichot for Growth/Energy, alongside Executive Chairman Andrew Forrest) framed FY2026 as delivered from 'a position of strength' — record shipments, an industry-leading cost position and a strong balance sheet — while acknowledging the Iron Bridge ramp-up has been slower than planned and warranted an impairment. The FY2027 outlook emphasises continued operational excellence and disciplined capital allocation, with decarbonisation (Green Grid, electrified fleet, Green Metal Project) positioned as a cost-reduction and resilience initiative rather than a new profit centre, and management continuing to argue the economics of moving away from fossil fuels are 'already clear' even as they lobby against Australian policy settings (the uncapped diesel fuel tax credit) that favour continued diesel use.
guidance.energy_capital_allocation_note: Historical company policy referenced 10% of NPAT as an approximate allocation guide for green energy initiatives; in practice Energy capex/opex has been highly variable (from over US$1 billion/year at the peak of the hydrogen buildout to the ~US$150m capex / ~US$300m opex guided for FY2027), reflecting the strategic retrenchment since mid-2024.

bull_case: Best-in-class Pilbara infrastructure and integration deliver a durable low-cost position (Hematite C1 of US$18.74/wmt in FY2026, near the bottom of the global cost curve), supporting a 51% group Underlying EBITDA margin even in a softening price environment

Fortress balance sheet (net gearing of just 4%, US$5.1 billion cash, US$6.1 billion total liquidity) gives Fortescue capacity to sustain dividends and growth capex through a cyclical downturn better than many peers, while still returning 50-80% of Underlying NPAT to shareholders

Green Grid decarbonisation program, once complete, offers a genuine, quantified cost-reduction pathway (up to 20% lower C1 costs targeted, ~US$100 million/year of diesel savings) that would extend Fortescue's cost-curve advantage independent of iron ore price moves

Meaningful pullback in the share price (down ~27-30% from its 52-week high to near 52-week lows around A$16-17 as of September 2026) may already discount much of the near-term iron ore price softness and Iron Bridge disappointment, offering an entry point if China demand or Iron Bridge execution stabilises

Optionality from copper (Cañariaco, Peru), Belinga hematite (Gabon) and green metal/green iron pilots (first hot metal achieved August 2026) provides long-dated diversification away from pure Pilbara hematite, funded from a low-cost, cash-generative core business
bear_case: Extreme single-commodity, single-region concentration leaves Fortescue with no offset if Chinese steel demand continues to soften or iron ore prices fall toward the US$85-95/t consensus range for 2026-2027, well below FY2026's realised US$91/dmt

New low-cost, high-grade Simandou (Guinea) supply ramping from ~15-20Mt in 2026 toward 120Mt by 2030 is a structural, multi-year headwind to seaborne iron ore prices and could widen the low-grade discount Fortescue's Hematite product already suffers relative to benchmark

Iron Bridge has been a persistent value-destroyer — a US$750 million impairment in FY2026, shipments still less than half of nameplate capacity, and full ramp-up not expected until ~2028 — casting doubt on Fortescue's ability to execute complex processing projects outside its core Hematite mine-rail-port model

Fortescue Energy's track record includes billions of dollars committed and then substantially written off or abandoned (Arizona Hydrogen, PEM50 Queensland, Gladstone electrolyser manufacturing), and while the Green Grid pivot is more disciplined, continued capital consumption (US$150m capex, US$300m opex guided for FY2027) against near-zero segment profitability remains a capital-allocation overhang and credibility question for management

Unresolved Yindjibarndi native title compensation appeal creates an open-ended legal and reputational liability — YNAC sought ~A$1.8 billion versus the A$150 million Fortescue has provided — with a precedent that could also affect the company's other Pilbara tenements and the broader Australian mining industry's native title exposure

Rising FY2027 cost guidance (Hematite C1 up to US$20.50-21.75/wmt, a 9-16% increase) shows the cost-curve advantage is not static, and combined with a strengthening AUD or renewed diesel price spikes could compress margins faster than volume growth can offset
